q.t: In 1284 King Edward I introduced the Statute of Rhuddlan. What did it do?
q.e: In 1284 King Edward I of England introduced the Statute of Rhuddlan, which annexed Wales to the Crown of England. Huge castles, including Conwy and Caernarvon, were built to maintain this power.
o: It annexed Wales to the Crown of England
It annexed Scotland to the Crown of England
It gave Wales its own parliament
It ended the Hundred Years War

q.t: Which battle, fought in 1314, left Scotland unconquered by the English?
q.e: In Scotland, the English kings were less successful. In 1314 the Scottish, led by Robert the Bruce, defeated the English at the Battle of Bannockburn, and Scotland remained unconquered by the English.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
The Hundred Years War actually lasted 116 years.
q.e: English kings also fought a long war with France, called the Hundred Years War, even though it actually lasted 116 years. One of the most famous battles was Agincourt in 1415.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: In 1348 a disease, probably a form of plague, came to Britain. This was known as the Black Death. One third of the population of England died and a similar proportion in Scotland and Wales.
o: The Black Death killed about one third of the population of England
The Black Death killed about two thirds of the population of England

q.t: What was the effect of the Black Death on the area of Ireland controlled by the English?
q.e: In Ireland, the Black Death killed many in the Pale and, for a time, the area controlled by the English became smaller.
o: The Pale became smaller for a time

q.t: Which TWO groups sat in the House of Lords when Parliament divided into two Houses?
q.e: The nobility, great landowners and bishops sat in the House of Lords. Knights, who were usually smaller landowners, and wealthy people from towns and cities were elected to sit in the House of Commons.
o: Wealthy people from towns and cities

q.t: How many Houses, called Estates, did the Scottish Parliament have in the Middle Ages?
q.e: A similar Parliament developed in Scotland. It had three Houses, called Estates: the lords, the commons and the clergy.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
In Scotland the legal system developed by codifying laws, that is, writing them down.
q.e: In England, judges developed 'common law' by a process of precedence, that is following previous decisions, and tradition. In Scotland, the legal system developed slightly differently and laws were 'codified', that is, written down.

q.t: Which TWO modern English words are given in the handbook as coming from Norman French?
q.e: Some words in modern English, for example 'park' and 'beauty', are based on Norman French words. Others, for example 'apple', 'cow' and 'summer', are based on Anglo-Saxon words.

q.t: Who wrote The Bruce, a poem in the Scots language about the Battle of Bannockburn?
q.e: In Scotland, many people continued to speak Gaelic and the Scots language also developed. A number of poets began to write in the Scots language. One example is John Barbour, who wrote The Bruce about the Battle of Bannockburn.

q.t: What is the currency of the UK, and how many pence are in a pound?
q.e: The currency in the UK is the pound sterling, symbol £. There are 100 pence in a pound. Coins are 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2; notes are £5, £10, £20 and £50.
o: The pound sterling, with 100 pence in a pound
The pound sterling, with 50 pence in a pound
The euro, with 100 cents in a euro
The pound sterling, with 20 pence in a pound

q.t: Which of these is NOT a denomination of UK banknote listed in the handbook?
q.e: The denominations of currency are coins: 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2; and notes: £5, £10, £20 and £50.

q.t: Where in the UK is Gaelic spoken?
q.e: In Scotland, Gaelic, again a different language, is spoken in some parts of the Highlands and Islands, and in Northern Ireland some people speak Irish Gaelic. In Wales, many people speak Welsh.
o: In some parts of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
According to the handbook, nearly 10% of the population has a parent or grandparent born outside the UK.
q.e: The UK today is a more diverse society than it was 100 years ago, in both ethnic and religious terms. Post-war immigration means that nearly 10% of the population has a parent or grandparent born outside the UK.

q.t: Which TWO of these cities are in Scotland, according to the handbook?
q.e: The handbook lists major cities of the UK. In Scotland these include Edinburgh, Glasgow, Dundee and Aberdeen. Norwich and Plymouth are listed among the cities of England.

q.t: Which church is the established Church of the state in England?
q.e: In England, there is a constitutional link between Church and state. The official Church of the state is the Church of England, called the Anglican Church in other countries and the Episcopal Church in Scotland and the United States. It is a Protestant Church.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: The monarch is the head of the Church of England. The spiritual leader of the Church of England is the Archbishop of Canterbury.
o: The monarch is the head of the Church of England
The Archbishop of Canterbury is the head of the Church of England

q.t: Who chairs the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland, and for how long?
q.e: In Scotland, the national Church is the Church of Scotland, which is a Presbyterian Church. It is governed by ministers and elders. The chairperson of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland is the Moderator, who is appointed for one year only.
o: The Moderator, appointed for one year only
The Archbishop of Edinburgh, appointed for life
The Moderator, appointed for five years
The monarch, for the length of the reign

q.t: In which TWO parts of the UK is there no established Church?
q.e: There is no established Church in Wales or Northern Ireland. In England the established Church is the Church of England; in Scotland the national Church is the Church of Scotland.

q.t: How often are general elections held, at a minimum?
q.e: MPs are elected at a General Election, which is held at least every five years. If an MP dies or resigns, there will be a fresh election, called a by-election, in his or her constituency.

q.t: What is the voting system used to elect MPs called?
q.e: MPs are elected through a system called 'first past the post'. In each constituency, the candidate who gets the most votes is elected. Elections to the European Parliament use a system of proportional representation.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
The House of Commons has powers to overrule the House of Lords, but these are not used often.
q.e: The House of Lords is normally more independent of the government than the House of Commons. The House of Commons has powers to overrule the House of Lords, but these are not used often.

q.t: What happens if an MP dies or resigns?
q.e: If an MP dies or resigns, there will be a fresh election, called a by-election, in his or her constituency.
o: A by-election is held in that constituency
A General Election is called immediately
The seat stays empty until the next General Election
The Prime Minister appoints a replacement

q.t: As part of the citizenship ceremony, what do new citizens do?
q.e: As part of the citizenship ceremony, new citizens pledge to uphold these values. The pledge includes giving loyalty to the United Kingdom, respecting its rights and freedoms, upholding its democratic values and observing its laws faithfully.
o: They pledge to uphold British values
They sit a second written examination
They are given a British passport free of charge
They must renounce all other citizenships in writing
